title: Smart Bird Feeder Cameras as a Gift: Birdbuddy Nook, Nook Solar and Home Compared
subtitle: A side-by-side look at the listed features of three camera feeders, what they do for free, and what the yearly Premium plan adds.
excerpt: A camera feeder sends close-up bird photos straight to a phone. Here is how Birdbuddy's Nook, Nook Solar and Home compare on paper, and what the $69.99-a-year Premium plan adds.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Many people love watching birds at the feeder, but the best visitors tend to arrive when you have stepped away, or they fly off the moment you reach for the binoculars. A smart bird feeder camera keeps watch for you. When a bird lands, it captures a photo or video and sends it to a smartphone.

That makes it a thoughtful holiday gift for a parent or grandparent who enjoys the backyard. Before you buy, though, it helps to know what works for free and what needs a yearly plan. Note that this is a comparison of the features and prices the maker lists. We have not tested these feeders.

The feeder holds seed like any other. A small camera records the visit and sends it over home Wi-Fi to the Birdbuddy phone app. There is no memory card slot, so everything is stored online in the company's cloud.

Here are three Birdbuddy models we cover. The Nook charges through a USB-C cable, the same small plug many newer phones use. The Nook Solar adds a solar roof. Birdbuddy's page says you never have to charge it, and it also says motion sensitivity lowers on cloudy days to save power. The Home has two solar panels, a 135-degree field of view and room for 6 cups of seed.

Free use works with the Nook line. On the free plan, you tap each photo to have the app identify the bird. Automatic identification, 2K Ultra video and a saved history of past visits need Premium. According to Birdbuddy's membership page, Premium costs $69.99 a year for one person or $98.99 a year for the Family plan. Prices change, so check the current price. Guests can watch the live camera feed only with the Family plan.
Other brands charge for bird identification too. In its tests, Reviewed found some charge about $4.49 a month, so it is worth checking each company's plan before comparing prices.

items: Power: a solar model means less charging. Our own thought is that this may matter if reaching the feeder means a ladder or icy steps. Remember that Nook Solar lowers its motion sensitivity on cloudy days.
The yearly cost: decide whether tapping each photo is fine, or whether automatic identification is worth $69.99 a year. Add that to the feeder price when budgeting.
Viewing: pictures arrive on a phone, not a TV. TechRadar's review of the earlier Birdbuddy Pro found portrait video suits a phone better than a television. The Home can show landscape or portrait.
Lag: the same TechRadar review, of the earlier 2025 Pro model, noted that notifications can lag.
Bigger birds: larger birds may struggle to land without the perch add-on. Birdbuddy sells a Perch Extender for $39.
Squirrels: squirrels can chew the housing and reach the seed. If you want a feeder with squirrel deterrents, these are not the right fit.
Returns: Birdbuddy's Nook page lists 90-day free returns on feeders and a money-back guarantee.
Setup help: you need Wi-Fi that reaches the yard and a smartphone with the app. Plan to help if your parent is not comfortable with apps.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

If you are giving this as a gift, consider setting it up together on a visit. Install the app on your parent's phone, connect the feeder to the home Wi-Fi, then choose a spot where the signal is strong and they can still see it from a favorite window. The Nook and the Home each come with a metal hanger and a universal pole mount.
Next, go through the notification settings. Since reviewers have noted that alerts can arrive late, it helps to set expectations: the photo may show up after the bird has gone.
If you pick Family Premium, guests can watch the live feed too, so far-away grandchildren can see the visitors, and the feeder becomes something to talk about on the next phone call.

This is a hobby gadget, not a safety device. It does not monitor a person's health or movement, and it is not a security camera, since it lacks the lights and alarms found on security-style cameras. Prices here come from the maker's pages, and other sellers may list different prices. In an emergency, call 911.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: For the person who already keeps a field guide by the window, a camera feeder can turn quiet mornings into a steady stream of small surprises. Pick the model that fits their yard, decide on the plan together, and set aside an afternoon to get it hanging. The birds will handle the rest.

products.name: Birdbuddy Nook
products.price: $99 (Basic Bundle, November 2026). The Essential Bundle is also $99 and includes one month of Family Premium, then $8.25/month billed yearly.
products.blurb: A good starting point for someone happy to recharge the feeder with a USB-C cable now and then. It takes 5MP photos and comes with a hanger, pole mount and a free hand-illustrated Bird Anatomy book.

products.name: Birdbuddy Nook Solar
products.blurb: Suits a parent who would rather not take the feeder down to charge it, thanks to a solar roof. It has the same 2K HDR camera as the Nook, and the page says motion sensitivity lowers on cloudy days to save power.

products.name: Birdbuddy Home
products.price: $199 (Basic, was $219, November 2026). Home plus Family Premium is also $199, with 1 month free, then $98.99/year.
products.blurb: Has dual solar panels, a 6-cup seed capacity and a 135° camera view. It can show the picture in landscape or portrait.
